 Former NC State football coach and alum Chuck Amato has died at 80.
 “Chuck Amato was NC State to his core,” North Carolina governor Josh Stein said in a social media post on Monday . “A two-sport athlete who came home to get the Pack back on the football map. He was a good coach and, by all accounts, a better man. May his memory be a blessing.”
 Other WRAL Top Stories
 Known for his bravado and barrel chest, Amato posted a 49-37 record at NC State and led the Wolfpack to five bowl games. His 49 wins are the fourth most in program history, behind Dave Doeren, Earle Edwards and Dick Sheridan. 
 "For seven seasons (2000-2006), the scrappy two-sport star and two-time NC State graduate from Easton, Pennsylvania, lived his dream, leading his alma mater to the best record (11-3) in school history in 2002, taking the program to five bowl games in his first six seasons and producing iconic players like quarterback Philip Rivers and linebacker Dantonio Burnette , among many others," NC State said in a statement posted on its athletics website. 
 Amato was head coach for the best season in program history when, in 2002, NC State won 11 games and finished No. 12 in the AP Top 25. Amato's time in Raleigh will forever be linked with quarterback Philip Rivers, who went on to rewrite the NC State record books.
 "Chuck was an amazing personality, and [I've] known him a long time. Met him when I was coaching at Wisconsin, and he was at Florida State as an assistant, and I coached against him many times," said NC State's current head coach Dave Doeren. "Just a huge personality, a great mentor to coaches and players alike, and a great alumnus."
 Prior to his time in Raleigh, Amato spent 21 seasons on Bobby Bowden's staff at Florida State, during the Seminoles' run of success, and eight seasons on staff with the Wolfpack. Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach and NC State alum Bill Cowher, who won a Super Bowl with the Steelers in 2006, said Amato was a big influence on him during his time in Raleigh.
 "You showed me tough love when I needed it & taught me Commitment, Sacrifice & Teamwork. You'll be missed, but your legacy will never be forgotten!" Cowher said in a statement posted to X, along with a photo of Cowher with Amato.
 RIP Coach Amato. Thank you for your influence and guidance in shaping me as a young LB from Western PA coming down to @PackFootball. You showed me tough love when I needed it & taught me Commitment, Sacrifice & Teamwork. You'll be missed, but your legacy will NEVER be forgotten! https://t.co/Lq1CPcsmyl
— Bill Cowher (@CowherCBS) October 19, 2026 
 Duke football coach Manny Diaz worked under Amato from 2000-2005 and spoke about his death at his weekly press conference on Monday. Diaz said he doesn't know of anyone who loved NC State more than Amato did.
 "Wouldn't be standing here today if it wasn't for Chuck Amato," Diaz said.
 He added: “Just the enthusiasm that he had, you know, you can't help (to) talk about Chuck without talking about the bravado. But he made people believe. He made his players believe.”
 As a player at NC State, Amato lettered in football and wrestling and was the captain of the Wolfpack defense in 1967. He also won two ACC titles as a wrestler, in 1966 and 1968.
 Amato retired in 2018 after coaching the Akron Zips for six seasons. 
 "Bobby Bowden preached for years the three 'F's – faith, family, and football – in that order," Amato said at the time of retirement. "My wife has a sister and brother who are not doing well right now, and I've got twin boys (grandsons) in my house."
 "I said to myself, 'Maybe it's time to go ahead and let someone else do it.' Just be happy and glad. I've been around. I've been to the top of the mountain twice, and if it wasn't for a wide left and a wide right, there'd be five of them (national championships). But I'm ready to retire, and I have to find something to do. If anybody out there has something they can give me, call me."
 Amato had been open about his health struggles in the past, speaking with WRAL more than a decade ago about his battle with throat cancer. 
 “[Cancer] makes you realize what life is all about,” he said before his time at Akron. “I’m going nutty right now, I want to coach so bad it’s killing me."
 Akron released statement about Amato.
 "We are grateful for his contributions to our football program from 2012-17 and the lasting impact he made on the student-athletes and colleagues he mentored throughout his distinguished coaching career," the university said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, former players and the countless individuals whose lives he touched."
